verdicts.reasoning: 'I heard a Negro play' and the third-person 'He did a lazy sway' set the speaker apart from the musician, so he is an observer and not the player.
'Pale dull pallor of an old gas light' makes the setting dim and worn. Lenox Avenue rules out a rural setting, and nothing in the line is festive or threatening.
The piano 'moan[s] with melody,' so it does produce a tune and the 'broken' reading fails. 'Moan' and 'poor' make it sound like it shares the sorrow.
'Swaying to and fro' and 'like a musical fool' describe a man lost in the music, and the 'rickety stool' shows the humble setting. The surrounding exclamations are admiring, which rules out contempt.
The musician's words are set in quotation marks and 'Sweet Blues!' is not, so it belongs to the speaker. 'Sweet' also points to admiration, not despair.
Quoting the song directly keeps the musician's own dialect, so the reader hears his sorrow in his own voice. The song is not addressed to the speaker and is not cheerful.
Line 24 says 'he sang some more,' so the thumping cannot mark the end of the playing. It is a pause before the darker second song.
In line 22 he resolves to 'put ma troubles on the shelf,' and in line 30 he says 'I wish that I had died.' He has clearly dropped the earlier resolve.
'Crooned' echoes the 'mellow croon' of line 2, framing the night's song. The other options have no support in the text.
'Slept like... a man that's dead' is a simile, and he has just 'went to bed,' so he is not literally dead. The comparison still recalls his wish to have died, as the key says.

The surrounding words are about age ('not so old', 'five-and-thirty') and his surprise at a 'thrill of boyish agitation'. So the 'temperate zone' means emotional calm in middle age. Option 3 brings in social storms, which are not part of this sentence.

'Tender sense of all it symbolized' and the 'garlanded nuptial door-posts' show his romantic hopes for the marriage. The hint of doubt comes only from the friend's remark at the end, not from Waythorn's feelings here.
'As he pictured her' marks the view as something he imagines, which supports the key. The narrator's irony is implied and never 'explicitly' stated, so option 0 is wrong.
Option 0 is directly contradicted by 'from temperament rather than circumstance'. The key matches 'he had been drawn to her by the unperturbed gayety', a quality his gray life lacks.

The sentence moves the narration from Waythorn's inner feelings to what society says about her, introduced by 'undercurrent of detraction'. Option 0 gets the direction of time backward, since the passage moves from the present into the past.
The remark is plainly ironic about how society hands out respectability, as 'took on an air of sanctity' confirms. No other option is plausible.
'Becoming' tells us the role flattered her, the way black crape sets off a rosy face. She is divorced, not widowed, and 'semi-widowhood' rules out a true widowhood.
'With your ears shut' undercuts Waythorn's claim that he went in 'with his eyes open'. It implies he has ignored warnings about her, which is the opposite of option 2.
The excerpt opens with him waiting at the hearth and then moves into her marital history. It never comes back to the present scene, so it is not a flashback that returns to the waiting husband.
Only 'a passport to the set whose recognition she coveted' links a marriage to social ambition. The other quotations are about her first elopement, her affection for Lily, or her nerves.

The cited details ('hearth,' 'pleasant room,' 'good dinner,' 'his own roof') are warm and domestic, and they frame his 'thrill of boyish agitation.' The illness is described as 'a light one' with 'favorable' symptoms, so nothing in these details creates dread.
The verse floats 'through his enjoyment' along with 'a tender sense of all it symbolized.' That is half-remembered literary romance, not doubt. Nothing in the text supports [0]'s secret doubt.

The passage calls the case 'a light one' with 'favorable' symptoms, which contradicts 'grave danger.' Lily is introduced as 'the child of Mrs. Waythorn's first marriage' and placed in his house on the wedding day, so her illness brings the first marriage into the new home at once.

'Wholly indifferent' is too strong and is contradicted by Lily being moved 'at Waythorn's desire.' The narrator's 'perhaps' and the theme of domestic charm support [3]'s 'partly... tender domesticity.'
The aside echoes society's offhand condescension ('unearthed somewhere') in free indirect style. It is not real narrative uncertainty, and the city is not central to the plot.
The sentence voices society's judgment ('it was easy'), not Waythorn's private prejudice. 'Nothing was known' turns ignorance into permission to condemn, which supports [1] directly.

'Took on an air' marks the sanctity as a performance. 'The role of the injured wife... as becoming to her as crape' confirms the irony, which rules out a genuine transformation and supports [1]'s skilful role-shifting.

The text says outright that 'it was not even suggested that Waythorn had supplanted his predecessor,' which rules out [0]. The 'True... Still' structure is a concession followed by a reversal, matching [3].

The outgrown, frayed coat set against the opal pin, the neatly knotted tie, the carnation and 'something of the dandy' points to elegance his circumstances can't support. Option 2 fails because those careful adornments show he cares a great deal about how he looks.

'Somehow felt' and the teachers' feeling it was 'scarcely possible to put into words' show Paul through the adults' vague impressions. Option 3 fails because the passage never gives Paul's thoughts about the faculty's hostility.
'Rancor and aggrievedness' and 'not a usual case' directly support the key. The other options are contradicted by the text.

The anecdote follows right after the 'real cause' the teachers can't name, and the passage then generalizes to 'physical aversion.' It is a concrete example of that aversion. No distractor has support.

The faculty feel the carnation is not 'properly significant of the contrite spirit,' so it stands for the opposite of contrition. Later it is 'flippantly red' and symbolizes his attitude. Option 0 reverses this.
'Fell upon him without mercy' and 'leading the pack' make the teachers a pack of predators attacking one quarry. No distractor fits.
'His set smile did not once desert him' while his fingers tremble nervously: the composure is a performance over real strain. Nothing suggests he is about to cry, so option 2 fails.

'Usually attributed' and 'as far as possible from boyish mirthfulness' put distance between the narrator and the teachers' reading. The earlier line about Paul feeling people 'might be watching him' supports anxious watchfulness. Option 2 misses the narrator's skeptical framing.

The key covers both the hostile point of view and the physical details (trembling fingers, twitching lips) that hint at fear. Option 2 generalizes to schools of the era and assumes Paul is artistic, which the excerpt never establishes.
'Confessed his perplexity' means he is bewildered. The father admits he does not understand his son. Nothing in the text says he takes the faculty's side against Paul.

'Suave' means polished composure, which clashes with a suspension hearing. Later details ('contempt,' 'set smile,' trembling fingers) show Paul knows exactly how serious it is, so 'unaware' does not fit.
'Peculiarly offensive in a boy' is a social judgment about what suits a boy. The belladonna comparison comes in the next sentence and is not part of the quoted remark.
The stem includes the qualification that the 'glassy glitter' is something the drug does not produce. That points past size to an unexplained intensity, and the word 'merely' rules out option 0.
The text says directly 'This was a lie,' which contradicts option 0. Lying to overcome friction is using deception as a practical tool.
The 'yet' clause sets the named offenses against a real cause that is hard to put into words: his manner and his contempt. Option 3 picks the stated offenses that the sentence pushes aside.
The behaviors happen in several classes ('In one class... in another... in another') and move from withdrawal to a mocking running commentary. No other option is supported by the text.
'His set smile did not once desert him' sets Paul's composure against the older boys who cried. Nothing suggests he is about to cry.

The keyed quotation shows anxious self-watching ('seeming to feel that people might be watching him') that sits under the performance. The running-commentary quotation shows performance with no sign of anxiety, so it supports only half the claim.

The phrases "appear before," "account for" and "misdemeanors" are legal language, and they set up a hearing in which Paul stands accused. The passage later says this "was not a usual case" and calls the hearing a "baptism of fire." Both contradict option 0's claim that the visit is unremarkable.

Right after "suave," the text describes the outgrown clothes and the frayed collar. It also says the faculty saw the carnation as "not properly significant of the contrite spirit." So "suave" marks composure that clashes with the penitence expected of him, not the narrator's open admiration. The narrator's tone is detached and somewhat critical.

"As though" makes belladonna a comparison, and the text adds that the glitter is one "which that drug does not produce." That rules out real drug use. Phrases like "hysterical brilliancy," "abnormally large" and "glassy glitter" all build a picture of unnatural intensity, which is the keyed answer.

"Overcoming friction" means getting past resistance, and Paul's polite lie to the Principal shows lying used to ease a conflict. Option 2 turns that meaning around. The oil image is a fair gloss on the figure of speech.
"Seemingly" ties the claim that Paul made no effort to hide his contempt to how he appeared. Option 0 says the teachers were deceived, which goes against "they all knew he felt."

"Involuntary" together with "physical aversion" and "shudder" points to an instinctive recoil. The teacher was guiding his hand, not threatening him, so nothing in the text suggests he feared being struck.

The comparison sets off the fact that Paul's "set smile did not once desert him." The trembling fingers and jerking hand show strain held in check, which is rigid self-control. Option 2's "well adjusted" doesn't fit those signs of strain.

content.text:
All seven keyed answers hold up, and none of the challenges works.

1. **Key clearly better.** The adversary is right that the text blocks any sense of foreboding. The symptoms are "favorable," the case "promised to be a light one," and the nurse "spoke as reassuringly." The hearth, the "pleasant room and the good dinner" and Waythorn's "boyish agitation" set up comfortable domestic expectation, and the gossip that follows plays against it. One flaw: the stem has a broken quotation ("the detail that (line 3)"). It should be fixed, but it doesn't change which answer is best.

2. **Key clearly better.** The image is "some old trail of verse" that floats "through his enjoyment." That makes it literary, private and idealizing. Nothing in it suggests worry that the marriage is a show staged for society.

3. **Key clearly better.** "Well-appointed" is a furnishing word, and it fits the idea of a polished, arranged composure. The text rules out a mask over anxiety: she has "perfectly balanced nerves," and "no woman ever wasted less tissue in unproductive worry."

4. **Key clearly better.** The careless aside, coming right after "whom Gus Varick had unearthed somewhere," carries society's condescending vagueness, echoed in the narrator's voice. Nothing in the text says Waythorn plans to question his wife.

5. **Key clearly better.** The sentence says believing the worst was "easy" because "nothing was known." That points to judgment based on convenience and ignorance, not to proof that Haskett was at fault.

6. **Key clearly better.** "This time" implies that no one took the husband's side before, which matches option 1. Option 0 is contradicted by the passage. Her grievances bear "the inspection of the New York courts," she takes on "an air of sanctity," and she confides in "the most scrupulous ears in town." Society had not turned against her.

7. **Key clearly better.** The passage calls it a "second separation," so Varick is alive. The tone is ironic, not sincere pity, and nothing predicts Waythorn's death. Option 3's double reading fits: she is really a divorcee who is given a widow's sympathy and dignity.

verdicts.reasoning: Reassuring details (favorable symptoms, light case) undercut foreboding; hearth, pleasant room, dinner, and boyish agitation establish comfortable expectation contrasted with later gossip. Stem has a garbled quotation but the answer is unaffected.
'Old trail of verse' floating through his enjoyment is literary, private idealization; no worry about public show is indicated.
'Well-appointed' is furnishing diction suggesting polished composure; text explicitly denies anxiety (balanced nerves, no unproductive worry).
The careless aside after 'unearthed somewhere' mimics society's condescension; nothing indicates Waythorn plans to question her.
Belief was 'easy' because 'nothing was known', exposing judgment from ignorance, not evidence of Haskett's fault.
'This time' implies the first husband had no defenders; society did not turn against Alice, who took on 'an air of sanctity'.
Varick is alive (separation); the term ironically lends a divorcee a widow's sympathy. Distractors lack support.

'Droning' and 'drowsy' go with 'syncopated' to describe a single tune: slow and heavy, but still rhythmic. Nothing in the poem sets a tired speaker against a lively player, and 'lazy sway' shows the playing itself is languid, not lively.

'Ebony' and 'ivory' are rich, precious materials, and they contrast with the 'poor piano' and 'rickety stool.' That contrast gives the performer dignity. Line 10 shows mastery ('made that poor piano moan with melody'), not unease.

Line 18 puts 'that Negro sing' and 'that old piano moan' side by side as parallel phrases, so the two become one voice. Option 1 says the piano alone carries the grief, which contradicts the student's claim of a shared voice.

'Put ma troubles on the shelf' means setting sorrows aside, and the shelf implies they are stored for later, not gone. It is a future intention ('gwine to'). The second song ('I ain't happy no mo'') shows he has not overcome anything.

The stars and moon going out marks how long the night has run, which fits 'far into the night.' Nothing in the text supports hope or relief: the poem ends with the blues still echoing in his head and a sleep 'like a man that's dead.'
